l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: This document is a sequence of Sherlock Holmes cases narrated or accompanied by Dr. John Watson, following Holmes’s return after the Reichenbach Fall through investigations involving murder, fraud, abduction, blackmail, stolen property, and political danger. It begins with Holmes’s reappearance to Watson during the Park Lane Mystery: Holmes explains his escape from Professor Moriarty, uses a wax likeness as bait, and captures Colonel Sebastian Moran, who killed Ronald Adair with an air-gun. Holmes then clears John Hector McFarlane when Jonas Oldacre’s supposed murder proves a revenge scheme staged by Oldacre himself. The cases broaden across England and beyond London. Holmes deciphers threatening dancing-men messages, exposing Abe Slaney after Hilton Cubitt is killed and Elsie Cubitt wounded. He saves Violet Smith from Jack Woodley, Williamson, and a forced marriage plot connected to her inheritance, while recognizing Bob Carruthers’s partial effort to protect her. He finds Lord Saltire, exposes James Wilder and Reuben Hayes in the Duke of Holdernesse’s secret kidnapping scheme, and resolves Captain Peter Carey’s death by proving Patrick Cairns acted in self-defense, freeing John Hopley Neligan. Holmes and Watson also confront Charles Augustus Milverton, destroying his blackmail papers after an unnamed woman kills him; recover the black pearl of the Borgias from Napoleon busts smashed by Beppo; and uncover Gilchrist’s theft of examination papers, aided by Bannister’s loyalty to Gilchrist’s father. Holmes solves Willoughby Smith’s killing through Anna and Professor Coram’s hidden history, then finds Godfrey Staunton mourning his secretly married wife, promising discretion. The later cases stress Holmes’s judgment as much as detection. At Abbey Grange, he rejects a fabricated burglary narrative, accepts Captain Crocker’s account that he killed Sir Eustace Brackenstall while defending Mary Fraser, and informally acquits him. The document ends with its largest political threat: a stolen letter could provoke European war. Holmes links it to Eduardo Lucas’s murder and Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope’s blackmail, recovers the letter, secretly restores it to the despatch-box, and preserves both the state’s security and Lady Hilda’s secret.

l: London, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: London is a city and a capital in Europe, viewed in accounts of crime. Colonel Sebastian Moran acquired an evil name there and remained a serious threat to Sherlock Holmes, who calls him London’s second most dangerous man. The murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair interests the city and dismays its fashionable world as Holmes returns from abroad. After Professor Moriarty’s death, Holmes finds London uninteresting to a criminal expert, though John Hector McFarlane travels through it for help. The story culminates in Beppo’s search for scattered Napoleon busts across districts including Kennington Road, Lower Brixton Road, and Pitt Street, while Holmes warns occupants of a remaining bust.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes is a living, six-foot-tall criminal investigator, detective, consulting detective, and criminal expert, based at and repeatedly returning to Baker Street, where he resides and works with his close friend, colleague, partner, and companion Dr. John Watson. He is famed for peculiar powers of deduction, uses deductive and inductive reasoning, studies physical traces, codes, maps, documents, and human conduct, and applies intense effort especially to strange, dramatic, or sympathetic cases rather than seeking large rewards or official position. After surviving the Reichenbach Fall and Professor Moriarty, Holmes spends nearly three years hidden, travelling in Tibet under the alias Sigerson, researching at Montpellier, visiting Khartoum, and concealing himself through disguises. He returns as an old book collector, learns an enemy remains in London, and uses a wax bust decoy to expose and secure the arrest of Colonel Sebastian Moran, whom he identifies as Ronald Adair’s murderer. With Moran removed, he is free to examine London again. His subsequent work unfolds through varied investigations with Watson and police contacts including Lestrade, Hopkins, and Martin. He exposes Jonas Oldacre’s staged death in the Norwood builder case; deciphers the dancing-men cipher, clears Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, and traps Abe Slaney; protects Violet Smith from an abduction and forced-marriage scheme; and resolves Lord Saltire’s disappearance by following bicycle tracks, recognizing a false cow-track trail, and confronting the Duke of Holdernesse. He also investigates Peter Carey’s death, attempts the recovery of blackmail letters from Charles Augustus Milverton, recovers the black pearl of the Borgias from a bust, identifies Gilchrist in the examination-paper theft, and investigates Willoughby Smith’s murder at Yoxley Old Place. Holmes’s methods include aliases such as Captain Basil and Escott, cultivated night vision, boxing, baritsu, revolvers when danger is expected, ciphers, and occasional burglary tools. He plays violin to soothe himself, smokes heavily, may forgo food during intense work, and keeps extensive biographical and other investigative materials. His work is marked by discretion, independence, readiness to confront danger, and a strong personal bond with Watson.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. John Watson is a doctor, medical practitioner, narrator, chronicler, and investigator closely bound to Sherlock Holmes as his friend, former companion, assistant, and professional partner. He keeps notes on unusual cases, writes investigations as stories rather than scientific exercises, and records events with admiration for Holmes while sometimes offering his own theories, doubts, or practical aid. He carries a revolver and check book, smokes tobacco, has irregular meals, and had helped wean Holmes from drug addiction. After selling his Kensington practice, Watson returns to share the Baker Street rooms with Holmes. Their renewed work begins after Watson investigates Ronald Adair’s murder, learns that Holmes is alive, and helps trap Colonel Sebastian Moran. Across subsequent cases, Watson accompanies Holmes to Norwood, Norfolk, Farnham, Mackleton, Sussex, Cambridge, Abbey Grange, Westminster, and elsewhere. He reads reports and messages, observes interviews and physical clues, assists surveillance and arrests, follows suspects, and records Holmes’s explanations. Watson also repeatedly contributes through his medical knowledge: reviving Thorneycroft Huxtable, examining injured people, reporting on Jack Woodley’s condition, and checking whether Violet Smith has recovered. His investigative efforts are not always praised, Holmes finds his position and methods in the cyclist inquiry inadequate, but Watson remains dependable in danger, helping stop a runaway dog-cart, restraining Patrick Cairns, holding Williamson at gunpoint, and assisting with the capture of Beppo. His loyalty sometimes leads him beyond ordinary legality. Though he disapproves of the planned burglary of Charles Augustus Milverton’s house, he prepares masks and rubber-soled shoes, stands guard, witnesses a woman’s revenge, helps burn documents, and escapes with Holmes. He safeguards the black pearl of the Borgias in a safe and is entrusted with confidential state information in the second-stain matter. At Abbey Grange, he serves as Holmes’s informal jury and finds Captain Crocker not guilty. By the end, he remains Holmes’s observant companion, sharing responsibility, secrecy, travel, and the continuing work of investigation.

l: the murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: In 1894 London, Ronald Adair was found shot dead in a locked room at 427 Park Lane; the unexplained crime led to a willful-murder verdict against unknown persons.

l: the Honourable Ronald Adair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Honourable Ronald Adair was a young aristocrat, the Earl of Maynooth’s second son, living with his mother and sister Hilda at 427 Park Lane. Formerly engaged to Miss Edith Woodley, he regularly and cautiously played card games at the Baldwin, Cavendish, and Bagatelle Clubs and was usually a winner. He played with Colonel Sebastian Moran and won considerable money; Holmes believed Adair discovered Moran cheating and threatened exposure. On March 30, 1894, Adair returned home at ten and was found fatally shot before 11:20 in his locked second-floor sitting-room. Moran killed him by firing an expanding bullet from an air-gun through the open front window.

s: No. 427, Park Lane is a residence on Park Lane with the Honourable Ronald Adair’s second-floor front sitting-room. Adair was found dead there after being shot through its open window; the locked door and lack of visible entry or escape traces made the case remarkable. Holmes attributes the shooting to Colonel Sebastian Moran.

l: the Park Lane Mystery, The Return of Sherlock Holmes

l: Park Lane, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Park Lane is a frequented thoroughfare in London with a nearby cab stand. It is associated with the shooting and murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair, who was shot from the open window of No. 427; no shot was heard and no ground disturbance was found.

Pursuing Sherlock Holmes in Switzerland, Moriarty confronted him at the Reichenbach Fall, tried to drag him over the brink, and fell to his death after Holmes escaped.

l: the Moriarty gang, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Moriarty gang, led by Professor Moriarty and including Colonel Sebastian Moran, was investigated after Moriarty's death; dangerous members remained free, forcing Sherlock Holmes to conceal his survival until only one enemy remained in London.

l: the Reichenbach Fall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Reichenbach Fall was the site where Professor Moriarty fell to his death and Sherlock Holmes appeared to die. Holmes secretly climbed to a ledge, evaded an accomplice who tried to kill him with rocks, and escaped over the mountains. The Reichenbach Fall is where Colonel Sebastian Moran previously attacked Holmes by dropping rocks over the cliff. Holmes refers to Moran’s attentions there when confronting him.

l: Baker Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Baker Street contains Sherlock Holmes’s rooms. After Holmes returns to London, Moran’s people watch the old rooms while Holmes uses a wax bust there as bait from Camden House. There Holmes and Dr. John Watson receive Stanley Hopkins, examine evidence, and prepare for Yoxley Old Place; later they discuss a missing letter with Lord Bellinger and Trelawney Hope.

l: Colonel Sebastian Moran, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Colonel Sebastian Moran, born in London in 1840, is the son of Sir Augustus Moran, educated at Eton and Oxford, and formerly served as a colonel in Her Majesty’s Indian Army and the 1st Bangalore Pioneers. A celebrated heavy-game shot, he served in several Indian campaigns, wrote two hunting books, and took part in a man-eating tiger hunt. After retiring, he developed a criminal career, became Professor James Moriarty’s chief of staff and bosom friend, and followed Moriarty in Switzerland. Holmes considers him London’s second most dangerous man. Moran is suspected, though never proved, to have caused Mrs. Stewart’s death; he shoots Ronald Adair after card cheating. At the Reichenbach Fall he attacks Holmes, then later fires an air-gun at Holmes’s apparent figure, is overpowered, and arrested.

l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Inspector Lestrade is an experienced plain-clothes detective, police inspector, and police official who works for Scotland Yard. He conducts official investigations, makes arrests, writes reports, and often works alongside Sherlock Holmes while retaining responsibility for police action. He arrives with officers when Holmes summons him and takes charge of Colonel Sebastian Moran’s arrest for the shooting of Ronald Adair; Holmes publicly credits Lestrade with the arrest, enhancing Lestrade’s reputation. In the Jonas Oldacre case, Lestrade leads the investigation, arrests John Hector McFarlane for Oldacre’s apparent murder, and initially considers the evidence conclusive despite Holmes’s objections. Once Oldacre’s deception is exposed, Lestrade recognizes that Holmes saved an innocent man and prevented a scandal, learns how the evidence was fabricated, and detains Oldacre for conspiracy or possibly attempted murder. Later, Lestrade investigates the destruction of Napoleon busts, a burglary, and an unidentified murder victim at 131 Pitt Street. He identifies the victim as Pietro Venucci, initially favors a Mafia-pursuit explanation, helps arrest Beppo, supplies Holmes with information, witnesses the recovery of the pearl, and praises Holmes on behalf of Scotland Yard. Finally, he brings Holmes into the room where Lucas was killed, investigates mismatched bloodstains under a drugget, and questions Constable MacPherson about a young woman who entered, fainted, and apparently moved it.

l: the police, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The police seek Colonel Sebastian Moran for Ronald Adair's shooting, enter an empty house when Holmes summons them, restrain Moran, and take him into custody. In another case, they build evidence against McFarlane but miss Oldacre's concealed room until Holmes's staged alarm reveals it.

l: Camden House, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: stands_opposite Baker Street Camden House stands opposite Holmes’s old quarters in Baker Street. Holmes and Watson hide there because it provides an excellent view of the lighted Baker Street window and the wax bust.

l: the empty house, The Return of Sherlock Holmes

Placed in Holmes’s Baker Street rooms, Mrs. Hudson repeatedly moves it so its shadow appears to be Holmes. It deceives watchers and draws Colonel Sebastian Moran’s fire, and is shot through the head instead of Holmes.

l: Von Herder's air-gun, The Return of Sherlock Holmes

Colonel Sebastian Moran used it murderously, including to fire at a wax bust; after Moran's arrest, it is destined to embellish the Scotland Yard Museum.

l: Moran's criminal career, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Moran's criminal career follows an initially honourable military career and includes suspected involvement in the death of Mrs. Stewart of Lauder. He later worked for Professor James Moriarty on high-class criminal jobs and became a dangerous enemy of Sherlock Holmes.

l: John Hector McFarlane, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: John Hector McFarlane is a young London solicitor, bachelor, Freemason, and asthmatic who lives with his parents at Torrington Lodge and is junior partner in Graham and McFarlane. Jonas Oldacre unexpectedly makes him beneficiary of a will and takes him to Norwood to examine documents, later showing him out through a French window. After staying at a Norwood hotel, McFarlane learns on his morning train that he is accused of Oldacre's murder and seeks Sherlock Holmes in fear of arrest. Police cite his bloody walking-stick, footprints, and an apparent right-thumb bloodprint; Lestrade arrests him. Holmes establishes that Oldacre is alive and that the evidence was manufactured: McFarlane had unknowingly left a thumb impression in soft wax, which Oldacre stained with blood to frame him.

l: Jonas Oldacre, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Jonas Oldacre is a fifty-two-year-old bachelor, retired builder, and well-known but secretive Lower Norwood resident who lives at Deep Dene House, where he owns a timber-yard and a house with a concealed hiding-place. He is described as a strange, ferret-like man with keen grey eyes, considerable reported wealth, and a malicious, vindictive, cunning, and cruel character. Though acquainted with John McFarlane's parents in youth, he targets McFarlane: he visits McFarlane's office, has him prepare a will leaving him most of Oldacre's property, then brings him to Deep Dene House to inspect documents. Oldacre stages his own apparent murder, fabricating evidence and arranging signs that McFarlane killed him and burned his body in the wood-pile. In fact, he hides in a secret room in the house. The scheme emerges amid evidence of financial trouble, creditor fraud, checks to Mr. Cornelius, a double existence under another name, and a planned flight with an assumed identity. Found alive, Oldacre calls the plot a practical joke, though it was designed to make an innocent man appear guilty; he is suspected of fraud and faces charges including conspiracy and possibly attempted murder.

l: Lower Norwood, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Jonas Oldacre [his residence is located there] Lower Norwood is the suburb where Jonas Oldacre lives and where the suspected crime, disappearance, and timber-yard fire occur. The Daily Telegraph reports that the events there may involve murder and arson.

l: Deep Dene House, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Deep Dene House is Jonas Oldacre’s large, brick-built modern villa in its own grounds at the Sydenham end of Deep Dene in Lower Norwood. It is central to Oldacre’s apparent murder: his unused bed, open safe, scattered papers, struggle-marked bedroom, fire, and incriminating evidence are found there. Holmes searches it, compares upper and lower corridors, finds a concealed room behind a lath-and-plaster partition, and Oldacre emerges during a simulated fire.

l: Blackheath, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a location [the location of John McFarlane's family home] Holmes visits Blackheath to investigate the sudden will and Oldacre's unexpected choice of heir. He learns from McFarlane's mother that Oldacre had been her former suitor, was cruel and vindictive, and had sent her a mutilated photograph as a curse.

l: Europe, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Europe is a militarized continent divided into a double league maintaining a military balance. After Lucas’s death, it shows no reported trouble for three days, yet a missing letter’s theft or publication could trigger dangerous international complications and affect its affairs.
